description: Amanita virosa, the European Destroying Angel, is a pure-white woodland mushroom and one of the most poisonous fungi known. Like its relatives in the death-cap group it contains amatoxins that cause delayed, often fatal liver and kidney failure.
edibilityNotes: Deadly poisonous; contains amatoxins (alpha-amanitin and related cyclic peptides). DELAYED, CUMULATIVE ONSET: symptoms are dangerously delayed, typically appearing 6-24 hours after ingestion (gastrointestinal phase of vomiting and diarrhea), often followed by a deceptive 'false recovery' period of 1-2 days before progressive, potentially irreversible liver and kidney failure. By the time symptoms appear, toxin is already absorbed and liver damage may be underway. A single fruiting body can be lethal. No safe preparation exists: cooking, drying, freezing, or parboiling does NOT destroy the toxins. Seek emergency medical care immediately on any suspicion of ingestion, even if the person currently feels well.
distribution: Widespread across temperate and boreal Europe; closely allied destroying-angel taxa (e.g. A. bisporigera, A. ocreata in North America) occur in Asia and the Americas.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Agaricus species (white edible mushrooms, e.g. horse and field mushrooms)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible Agaricus species have pink-to-chocolate-brown gills that darken with age and a brown spore print, and lack a volva. Amanita virosa has persistent white (free) gills, a white spore print, and a distinctive sac-like basal volva. Always check the base of the stem for a volva.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Edible puffballs (immature button stage)
dangerousLookalikes.note: At the immature 'egg' stage the volva-enclosed Amanita button can resemble a small puffball. Cutting it vertically reveals the silhouette of a developing capped, gilled mushroom inside; a true puffball is uniformly solid white flesh throughout with no internal structure.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita phalloides (Death Cap)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Another deadly amatoxin-containing Amanita, distinguished by its greenish to olive- or yellow-tinged cap, whereas A. virosa is pure white. Both are lethal, so this distinction matters only for identification, not for safety.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Volvariella / Volvopluteus species (volvate edible mushrooms)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Some edible volvate species also have a basal volva, but they produce a PINK to salmon spore print and pinkish mature gills, versus the white gills and white spore print of A. virosa. A spore print is essential when a volva is present.
